00:47 Maya: first, high-level accuracy tradeoffs. INT8 is mature, good perf wins, but needs careful calibration for layernorm and attention. FP8 can keep more dynamic range, but hardware support is newer. GPTQ often gives best size/quality tradeoff for LLMs without retraining; AWQ is promising for lower bitwidths with preserved accuracy but has quirks.
01:09 Priya: can you give concrete numbers? like perplexity or instruction-following drop?
01:14 Ethan: rough rules of thumb from our bench: GPTQ (4-bit) on LLaMA-style models ->~1-3% relative quality regression on our evals; AWQ sometimes closes that gap on some models but can be inconsistent. INT8 tends to have ~2-5% depending on layer folding and per-channel scales. FP8 usually <1-2% but needs hardware support and can be unstable for very deep layers if kernel implementations are experimental.
01:40 Marcus: how about throughput and memory? we care about latency tail for chat.
01:44 Ethan: quantization mainly reduces memory / cache pressure. GPTQ / AWQ 4-bit reduces KV cache size ~2.5-3x compared to FP16 which improves cache hit behavior. For throughput: on A100, INT8/FP8 kernels can give ~1.5-2.2x token/sec depending on sequence length and batch. For latency we see improvements but batching policies matter; small-batch (<8) interactive latency improves less than bulk throughput.
02:12 Priya: you mentioned KV cache - any surprising interactions with quantized weights?
02:16 Ethan: yes. KV cache is mostly activations stored per token; quantized weights reduce working set so you can fit larger KV caches in GPU memory, which indirectly reduces recomputation and offloading. caveat: some runtime paths use fused kernels that expect FP16 weights; if we use certain GPTQ kernels they might force different attention kernel paths - so latency can sometimes increase if the kernel isn't optimized.
02:43 Maya: example: with AWQ on our engineer bench we saw 30% gen throughput improvement for throughput-mode batching but a 5-10% tail-latency regression in the 99th when small-batch spikes hit unoptimized kernels.
02:58 Marcus: is there a fallback plan? we need graceful degradation since chat is customer-facing.
03:02 Ethan: Redwood runtime supports routing policies and automatic fallback to a higher-precision variant - e.g., AWQ->FP16 or GPTQ-quantized variant with different kernel. can set canary routes and A/B to verify QoE.
03:13 Sophie: regarding accuracy regressions, are there known failure modes on instruction following or hallucinations?
03:18 Ethan: yes, lower-bit quant can amplify rare token errors especially in few-shot or chain-of-thought prompts. GPTQ tends to preserve logits order better, AWQ sometimes needs per-layer remapping for certain attention matrices. we recommend targeted evals: instruction-following, safety prompts, and proprietary prompt-sets.
03:36 Priya: will you run the evals or do we run them?
03:39 Maya: we'll do an initial Redwood-run on a sample of your prompts, then we hand you the scripts to run at scale in your VPC. for the POC we'll ask for ~2k-5k representative inputs.
03:49 Marcus: network wise, because of egress limits we prefer Redwood SEs to run bench inside our staging VPC. is that possible?
03:54 Ethan: yes - we'll need an ephemeral access key and an SSH jump or a dedicated test instance. we'll coordinate with Marcus.
04:02 Priya: curious about calibration - do you use per-channel scales, symmetric or asymmetric quant?
04:06 Ethan: we typically use per-channel asymmetric for weights and activation-aware per-tensor scaling for activations; GPTQ uses Hessian-based per-channel calibration for better fidelity. AWQ often uses hybrid schemes. these choices affect both accuracy and kernel throughput.
04:24 Maya: also note compile/kernel selection: runtime will pick different kernels based on sequence length distribution. short-chat workloads use fused kernels optimized for low-latency; long-context retrieval pipelines use different tiled matmul kernels that favor throughput. quantized kernels need the right GEMM path to shine.
04:43 Sophie: do you have a recommended starting config for Helion's stack?
04:46 Ethan: for mixed A100/H100 I'd recommend: a GPTQ 4-bit for model family X (low regression), AWQ experiment for throughput-critical endpoints, FP8 candidate for batch analytics endpoints, and keep an FP16 variant for sensitive endpoints (payments, legal). enable auto-fallback and set canary to 5% traffic first.
05:06 Priya: procurement question - what's the impact on cost?
05:09 Maya: quant reduces GPU memory and effective instance needs; rough estimate: 30-60% cost reduction on token compute depending on workload and kernel maturity. we'll share a more granular spreadsheet.
05:20 Marcus: logging & compliance - does Redwood store any prompts or are they in our VPC?
05:24 Ethan: with Redwood Private, control plane is customer managed. logs and traces can be kept in your storage; we can configure audit export to your SIEM, no customer data leaves your VPC unless you opt-in.
05:34 Maya: quick demo note - we'll attach a short doc showing the benchmark harness we use and the parameter file for GPTQ/AWQ conversion.
